module_title: Introduction to Physical Quantities and the SI System
introduction: Physics is the study of the natural world based on measurements. Any quantity that can be measured and expressed in numbers is called a 'Physical Quantity' (e.g., length, mass, velocity). To measure these quantities, we need standard reference points called 'Units'.

core_concepts.title: Fundamental vs. Derived Quantities
core_concepts.description:
1. Fundamental Quantities: These are independent and do not rely on any other quantity. There are exactly 7 fundamental quantities in Physics. 
2. Derived Quantities: These are formed by combining fundamental quantities (e.g., Speed = Distance / Time).

core_concepts.title: The 7 Fundamental SI Units
core_concepts.description:
In 1971, the internationally accepted SI system (Système International) defined 7 base units: 
1. Length -> Meter (m) 
2. Mass -> Kilogram (kg) 
3. Time -> Second (s) 
4. Electric Current -> Ampere (A) 
5. Temperature -> Kelvin (K) 
6. Luminous Intensity -> Candela (cd) 
7. Amount of Substance -> Mole (mol).

core_concepts.title: Supplementary Units
core_concepts.description:
Apart from the 7 base units, there are 2 supplementary units used for measuring angles: 
1. Plane Angle -> Radian (rad) 
2. Solid Angle (3D angle) -> Steradian (sr).

important_entities.name: Temperature in Kelvin
important_entities.significance: In everyday life, we use Celsius (°C), but the SI unit of temperature is strictly 'Kelvin' (K). Remember: $K = °C + 273.15$. There is no 'degree' symbol used with Kelvin.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Because the word 'Year' is in it, students often assume a Light Year is a unit of Time. FALSE. A Light Year is a unit of DISTANCE (the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year, which is about $9.46 \times 10^{15}$ meters).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Many Kings Try Catching Little Angry Mice
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Mass (kg), Kelvin (Temp), Time (s), Candela (Intensity), Length (m), Ampere (Current), Mole (Substance).

exam_strategy_tips: Direct Question in SSC/Railways: 'What is the SI unit of Luminous Intensity?' Answer: Candela (cd).
